morphology.summary: Not a single organelle but a whole SYSTEM of three distinct protein fibre types threading through the cytoplasm of every eukaryotic cell: microfilaments (actin), intermediate filaments, and microtubules. Together they give the cell its shape, let it crawl and change shape, hold organelles in place, and serve as the tracks that motor proteins walk cargo along. The single most important teaching fact is that the three fibre types are not just 'more of the same' at different sizes - they are built from completely different proteins, have different mechanical roles, and above all have unmistakably different, easily-checkable diameters: thin actin (~7 nm) < medium intermediate filaments (~10 nm) < thick, hollow microtubules (~25 nm). Getting that size ordering visually obvious is the entire point of this poster.
morphology.kind: cytoplasmic filament system of eukaryotic cells (three distinct polymer types), not a membrane-bound organelle - it has no boundary of its own and permeates the whole cytoplasm
morphology.microfilaments_actin: The thinnest fibres, about 7 nm in diameter. Each filament is a helical polymer of two protofilaments of the globular protein G-actin twisted around each other like a two-stranded 'string of beads' or rope (F-actin = filamentous actin). Actin filaments are polarised (a fast-growing 'plus/barbed' end and a slow-growing 'minus/pointed' end) and are concentrated in a dense meshwork just under the plasma membrane called the cell cortex, and inside surface protrusions such as filopodia (thin spikes) and lamellipodia (sheet-like fronts) that let a cell crawl. Constant assembly at the plus end and disassembly at the minus end ('treadmilling'), often together with the motor protein myosin, generates the pushing/pulling forces of cell crawling, cell-surface shape changes, and cytokinesis (the actin-myosin contractile ring that pinches a dividing cell in two).
morphology.intermediate_filaments: Medium-thickness fibres, about 10 nm in diameter - intermediate between actin and microtubules, which is literally where the name comes from. Unlike actin and microtubules, which are each built from one globular protein (actin or tubulin), intermediate filaments are built from a diverse family of elongated, rod-shaped fibrous proteins (keratins in epithelial cells, vimentin in mesenchymal cells, desmin in muscle, neurofilament proteins and others in neurons, lamins inside the nucleus) that dimerise, pair into staggered tetramers, and bundle into thicker ropes with no inherent polarity (no plus/minus end) and no attached motor proteins. They are the cytoskeleton's tension-bearing cables: mechanically the toughest and most durable of the three fibre types, resistant to stretching, and the ones that anchor at desmosomes and hemidesmosomes (cell-cell and cell-matrix junctions) to spread mechanical stress across a whole tissue - which is why they are especially dense in tissues under constant mechanical stress, like skin.
morphology.microtubules: The thickest fibres, about 25 nm in diameter, and the only ones of the three that are HOLLOW tubes rather than solid strands. A microtubule wall is built from 13 parallel protofilaments, each a head-to-tail chain of alpha-tubulin/beta-tubulin heterodimers, arranged side by side around a central hollow lumen/bore roughly 15 nm across - so a cutaway or broken end must show a visible open channel down the middle, and the surface should read as a finely ridged/fluted lattice of 13 parallel strands, not a smooth rod. Microtubules are polarised (fast-growing plus end, slower minus end anchored at the organizing centre) and undergo 'dynamic instability' - rapid, stochastic switching between growth and catastrophic shrinkage - which is the molecular basis of the 'constantly built up and torn down' behaviour of the whole cytoskeleton. Most microtubules radiate outward through the cytoplasm from the centrosome (the microtubule-organizing centre, MTOC), typically located near the nucleus, with their minus ends anchored there and their plus ends extending toward the cell periphery.
morphology.centrosome_mtoc: The main microtubule-organizing centre (MTOC) in animal cells, usually positioned adjacent to the nucleus. It nucleates and anchors the minus ends of most cytoplasmic microtubules, which then radiate outward from it in a characteristic star/aster pattern. During mitosis the centrosome duplicates and the two copies organize the mitotic spindle, whose microtubules attach to and pull the duplicated chromosomes apart. The centrosome itself is not a bounded organelle with a membrane; it is a dense, pericentriolar protein matrix (structurally containing a pair of centrioles, which are themselves built from a ring of triplet microtubules, though the centrioles are a fine architectural detail, not required for the composition here) that acts as an anchor/nucleation site.
morphology.motor_proteins: Two large families of ATP-powered motor proteins walk along microtubules in opposite directions, hauling membrane vesicles, organelles and other cargo: kinesins generally walk toward the microtubule plus end (outward, toward the cell periphery) and dyneins generally walk toward the minus end (inward, toward the centrosome). Both have a compact, two-headed, two-legged shape: a pair of globular motor 'head' domains that grip the microtubule surface and take alternating steps (a hand-over-hand walk) along one of its 13 protofilament tracks, connected via a stalk/neck to a tail domain that binds the cargo (often via an adaptor, schematically a membrane-bound vesicle). This is the concrete mechanical picture behind 'transport rails': the microtubule is the track, the motor is a two-legged walker striding along it, and the cargo is a vesicle carried on its back.
morphology.dynamics_turnover: None of the three fibre systems is a fixed, permanent scaffold like a skeleton of bones. All three are constantly remodelled: actin filaments treadmill (grow at one end, shrink at the other) on a timescale of seconds to minutes, microtubules undergo dynamic instability (rapid stochastic growth/catastrophic shrinkage) on a similar timescale, and even intermediate filaments, the most stable of the three, are subunit-exchanging polymers rather than permanently fixed structures. This constant turnover is what lets a cell rebuild its shape, crawl, divide and rebuild its transport network from one moment to the next - the opposite of a rigid, static frame.
morphology.mitotic_role: During cell division, microtubules of the mitotic spindle attach to the kinetochores of the duplicated, condensed chromosomes and physically pull the sister chromatids apart to opposite poles of the dividing cell - the direct, concrete answer to 'how do microtubules act as railway tracks that also handle chromosome separation.'
morphology.listeria_hijack: The intracellular bacterial pathogen Listeria monocytogenes hijacks the actin (not microtubule) half of the host cytoskeleton to move within and between cells. A single bacterial surface protein, ActA, displayed at one pole of the bacterium, activates the host cell's Arp2/3 actin-nucleating complex and recruits other host actin-regulatory proteins (profilin, Ena/VASP), triggering explosive, localized polymerization of a branched actin network that forms a 'comet tail' behind the bacterium. Continuous actin polymerization at the bacterium-tail interface pushes the bacterium through the cytoplasm at up to tens of micrometres per minute; on reaching the plasma membrane the bacterium pushes out a thin, actin-filled protrusion into a neighbouring cell, which is pinched off and engulfed, letting the bacterium spread from cell to cell without ever leaving the cytoplasm or being exposed to extracellular antibodies. This is a clean illustration of the broader teaching point - the cytoskeleton is a dynamic, buildable/rebuildable system, not a fixed frame, and that dynamism is exactly what a pathogen can exploit.
morphology.colour_note: None of the three fibre types has any intrinsic colour; the classic real-world image of the cytoskeleton is a fluorescence micrograph in which each fibre type is labelled with a different coloured fluorescent antibody/dye and the nucleus is counterstained separately - i.e. the colours seen in micrographs are stains, not a natural property of the structures. All colour in the illustrated teaching plates below is likewise a chosen convention, used consistently to keep the three fibre types and the motor protein easily distinguishable and to make the thin/medium/thick size relationship legible at a glance.

structures.note: THINNEST fibre (~7 nm) - two thin protofilament strands of G-actin twisted round each other like a beaded rope. Concentrated in a dense mesh just under the plasma membrane (the cell cortex) and inside surface protrusions. Must read as visibly the thinnest of the three fibre types.

MEDIUM-thickness fibre (~10 nm), between actin and microtubules - the most rope-like/braided in appearance, no polarity. Bundled rope of coiled fibrous-protein subunits; bears tension and anchors at cell-cell junctions. Must read as visibly thicker than actin but thinner than a microtubule.

THICKEST fibre (~25 nm) and the only HOLLOW one - a tube built from 13 parallel protofilaments of alpha/beta-tubulin dimers around a visible central bore. Radiates from the centrosome. Show an open, hollow channel wherever a tip or cut end is visible, and a finely ridged/fluted 13-strand lattice on the surface - never a smooth solid rod.
The dense, unbounded (no membrane) protein hub near the nucleus from which most microtubules radiate outward, minus-end-in, in a star/aster pattern.

A small two-legged, two-headed walker striding hand-over-hand along a microtubule, hauling a membrane vesicle (cargo) on its tail domain - the concrete image behind 'transport rail'. Must be shown ON a microtubule, in a clear walking pose, never floating free or on the wrong fibre type.

The dense actin-microfilament meshwork directly under the plasma membrane that shapes the cell surface and powers crawling; not a separate structure from the microfilaments themselves, but worth labelling as the zone where they concentrate.

do_not_draw: Do NOT draw microtubules as solid, smooth rods. They are HOLLOW tubes with a visible open bore/lumen at any cut end or tip, and a finely ridged 13-protofilament lattice on the surface - a solid rod is the single most common and most damaging error for this subject.

Do NOT draw all three fibre types at the same thickness. The whole teaching point is the size ordering thin-actin < medium-intermediate-filament < thick-microtubule; if the three look interchangeable in thickness the picture has failed at its one job.

Do NOT draw the cytoskeleton as a rigid, fixed, permanently-built frame like a skeleton of bones. It is constantly assembled and disassembled (actin treadmilling, microtubule dynamic instability) - convey a sense of active, dynamic construction, not a static cage.

Do NOT draw DNA, chromosomes, chromatin or a nucleus interior as part of the cytoskeleton itself. Microtubules PULL chromosomes apart during division (a fine detail to mention in text) but chromosomes/DNA are not cytoskeletal structures and should not be drawn as such filaments.

Do NOT draw a bacterial flagellum, or any rotary corkscrew/propeller structure. That is a bacterial motility organelle built from flagellin, structurally and functionally unrelated to any of the three eukaryotic cytoskeletal fibre types in this poster.

Do NOT compose actin filaments as a smooth solid ribbon or single strand - they are a two-stranded twisted/beaded rope, distinct from the braided-rope look of intermediate filaments and from the ridged hollow tube look of microtubules.
Do NOT give intermediate filaments a directional arrow or polarity marker (a plus/minus end) - unlike actin and microtubules, they have no inherent polarity.

Do NOT anthropomorphise the fibres (no faces, eyes or limbs) in the textbook/sem/3d/watercolor styles - a friendly face belongs only on the separate colouring page. No text, letters, numbers, labels, scale bars, arrows-with-text or watermarks baked into any image.

colour_legend.microfilament: #C9484F (dusty coral-red), thinnest fibres, concentrated as a dense mesh just under the outer edge/cortex and inside any surface protrusions
colour_legend.intermediate_filament: #4E8B72 (soft teal-green), medium-thickness rope-like bundles crossing the cytoplasm and anchoring at the cell edge/junctions
colour_legend.microtubule: #3A7CA5 (steady mid-blue), thickest fibres, radiating outward from the centrosome, drawn with a visible hollow bore at any cut end and a finely ridged surface
colour_legend.centrosome: #8B7355 (muted grey-brown), a small dense hub near the nucleus where the microtubules converge
colour_legend.motor_protein: #E8A33D (warm amber-gold), tiny two-legged walker on a microtubule carrying a paler vesicle blob as cargo
colour_legend.note: None of the three fibre types has any natural colour - the classic real reference image is a fluorescence micrograph where each is tagged with a different coloured stain. The palette here is a teaching convention chosen purely to keep the thin/medium/thick size relationship and the three distinct fibre identities legible at a glance.

sources.title: "The Actin Cytoskeleton" - The Cell: A Molecular Approach, Cooper (NCBI Bookshelf NBK9908)
sources.note: Actin filaments (microfilaments) are ~7 nm helical polymers of two twisted protofilaments of globular G-actin, polarized with distinct plus/minus ends, concentrated in the cell cortex beneath the plasma membrane.

sources.title: "Actin, Myosin, and Cell Movement" - The Cell: A Molecular Approach, Cooper (NCBI Bookshelf NBK9961)
sources.note: Actin-myosin interactions drive cell crawling, the contractile ring of cytokinesis, and other nonmuscle cell movements; constant polymerization/depolymerization (treadmilling) underlies these dynamic shape changes.

sources.title: "Intermediate Filaments" - The Cell: A Molecular Approach, Cooper (NCBI Bookshelf NBK9834)
sources.note: Intermediate filaments are ~10 nm in diameter, intermediate between actin filaments (~7 nm) and microtubules (~25 nm); built from a diverse family of fibrous proteins (keratins, vimentin, desmin, neurofilament proteins, lamins) rather than a single protein type, and lack inherent polarity.

sources.title: "Microtubules" - The Cell: A Molecular Approach, Cooper (NCBI Bookshelf NBK9932)
sources.note: Microtubules are hollow, rigid rods ~25 nm in diameter, walls built from 13 protofilaments of alpha/beta-tubulin heterodimers; polarized, generally organized with minus ends anchored at the centrosome (MTOC) and plus ends extending to the cell periphery; undergo dynamic instability.

sources.title: "Microtubule Motors and Movements" - The Cell: A Molecular Approach, Cooper (NCBI Bookshelf NBK9833)
sources.note: Kinesins and dyneins are the two families of microtubule motor proteins; kinesin generally moves toward the microtubule plus end and dynein toward the minus end, powering vesicle/organelle transport, chromosome movement, and ciliary/flagellar beating.

sources.title: "Molecular Motors" - Molecular Biology of the Cell, Alberts et al. (NCBI Bookshelf NBK26888)
sources.note: Minus ends of a typical interphase microtubule array are anchored at the centrosome near the cell center, plus ends extend to the periphery; centripetal cargo movement uses minus-end-directed dynein, centrifugal movement uses plus-end-directed kinesins; dyneins are among the largest and fastest known molecular motors.

sources.title: "The actin comet guides the way: how Listeria actin subversion has impacted cell biology..." - Kuehn et al., Cellular Microbiology 2020
sources.note: Listeria monocytogenes displays the surface protein ActA at one bacterial pole, activating the host Arp2/3 complex (plus profilin and Ena/VASP proteins) to nucleate a branched actin comet tail; continuous actin polymerization propels the bacterium through the cytoplasm and into actin-filled protrusions that spread it to neighbouring cells without leaving the cytosol.

reference_micrograph_candidates_plan: See render.md section 2 for the chosen candidate and its verification: a classic immunofluorescence light-microscopy image (NIGMS/NIH, Torsten Wittmann, Nikon Small World 2003 first place) showing actin (labelled purple/lavender), microtubules (labelled yellow, visibly radiating from the centrosome near each nucleus), and nuclei (labelled green) in cultured mammalian cells - stated plainly as a stained fluorescence light-micrograph, not an electron micrograph, and the colours as stains rather than natural.
